teaching.task: # Maths S11 D13: How do the range and standard deviation measure spread? Highest minus lowest, its weakness with one extreme value, and σ as roughly the typical distance from the mean, read from the calculator's statistics mode (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: The simplest measure of spread is the range. It's the highest value minus the lowest value. Bus A's latest day was five minutes, and its earliest was three, so its range is five minus three, two minutes. Bus B's range is eight minus nought, eight minutes. A bigger range means more spread, so Bus B is less consistent. The range is quick, but notice what it uses. Only two values, the highest and the lowest. Everything in between is ignored. Its units are the data's units, here minutes. That's the range's weakness. Say Bus A breaks down one day and arrives fifteen minutes late. The other five days are the same, three to five minutes late. But the range jumps from two to twelve, making Bus A look less consistent than Bus B. The range also ignores everything between the two ends. We need a measure of spread that uses every value. The standard deviation does that. Measure each value's distance from the mean. That's called its deviation. Bus A's deviations are tiny, one, nought, nought, nought, one, nought. Bus B's are big, four, three, two, two, three, four. The standard deviation combines all those distances into one number, roughly the typical distance of the values from the mean. It's written with the Greek letter sigma. For Bus A, sigma is about nought point five eight minutes. For Bus B, about three point one one minutes. Meet Bus C. Nought, four, four, four, four, eight. Its range is eight, the same as Bus B's, but most of its days sit right on the mean, so its sigma is two point three one. Sigma sees a difference the range missed. A bigger sigma means the values usually sit further from the mean, so they're less consistent. Every value counts, odd ones too. Put Bus A's breakdown day back, and its sigma jumps to four point one four, because that one big distance counts heavily. The measure that ignores the extremes is the interquartile range, the IQR, coming soon. Sigma has the same units as the data, minutes here.

scenes.teachingReason: The simplest measure of spread is the range. It's the highest value minus the lowest value. Bus A's latest day was five minutes, and its earliest was three, so its range is five minus three, two minutes. Bus B's range is eight minus nought, eight minutes. A bigger range means more spread, so Bus B is less consistent. The range is quick, but notice what it uses. Only two values, the highest and the lowest. Everything in between is ignored. Its units are the data's units, here minutes.

scenes.teachingReason: The standard deviation does that. Measure each value's distance from the mean. That's called its deviation. Bus A's deviations are tiny, one, nought, nought, nought, one, nought. Bus B's are big, four, three, two, two, three, four. The standard deviation combines all those distances into one number, roughly the typical distance of the values from the mean. It's written with the Greek letter sigma. For Bus A, sigma is about nought point five eight minutes. For Bus B, about three point one one minutes. Meet Bus C. Nought, four, four, four, four, eight. Its range is eight, the same as Bus B's, but most of its days sit right on the mean, so its sigma is two point three one. Sigma sees a difference the range missed. A bigger sigma means the values usually sit further from the mean, so they're less consistent. Every value counts, odd ones too. Put Bus A's breakdown day back, and its sigma jumps to four point one four, because that one big distance counts heavily. The measure that ignores the extremes is the interquartile range, the IQR, coming soon. Sigma has the same units as the data, minutes here.

Students whose phone charged elsewhere averaged eight point one three hours, with a sigma of nought point seven eight. Which group sleeps more, and more steadily? And how would you write that, with numbers and a spreadsheet? That's next.
